motivation: In 2009 Miyasaka first used organometal halide perovskites as light absorbers in photovoltaic cells. In 2012 Park demonstrated a stable solid-state perovskite cell with about 9% efficiency, and Snaith showed that perovskites work as ambipolar semiconductors with long carrier diffusion lengths in thin-film planar devices. Together these steps created a new class of solution-processed semiconductors. Their defect tolerance, sharp absorption edge and tunable bandgap overturned the long-held assumption that high-performance optoelectronics requires near-perfect crystals. In little more than a decade, efficiencies have risen above 26% in single junctions and above 33% in perovskite–silicon tandems, and commercial production has begun. As with gallium nitride, patient materials science on a once-unfashionable compound opened new semiconductor physics and a technology of great value for sustainable energy. This is the kind of discovery Alfred Nobel meant to reward: one that brings the greatest benefit to humankind.
